info.desc: By January 1977, punk had become a major media phenomenon in the UK. On 25 January 1977, The Clash signed to CBS Records for £100,000, a remarkable amount for a band that had played a total of about thirty gigs and almost none as a headliner. podcast.body: The band recorded their self-titled debut album at CBS Studio 3, featuring songs based on real people and events from their experiences in London during the punk years. The back cover of the album features a photograph depicting the events of the Notting Hill riot from August 30, 1976. "When they entered CBS Studio 3 to record their self-titled debut album, they were armed with a bunch of songs based on real people and real events."

podcast.body: This self-titled album was recorded over three weekends and became a big hit in Britain. Despite having a worldwide deal with CBS Records, the label initially refused to release it in North America, deeming it "too raw, abrasive, crude, and political for American tastes" during the disco era. North American fans were forced to buy higher-priced British import versions, which sold 100,000 copies, making it the biggest-selling import at the time. CBS finally released a "somewhat watered down version with a different track listing" in 1979. The album's cover only features Joe Strummer, Mick Jones, and Paul Simonon because at the time the photo was shot, the band didn't have a full-time drummer after Terry Chimes split.
